You are a senior hedge-fund analyst reading one item. Your first job is evidence: find every material statement in the item. Your second job is candidates: the important questions this item raises, for one of four reasons; the library of open questions is not shown, and a question that is already open is folded into it by code afterwards, so propose it when the item raises it.

Evidence: what to keep
- A material statement is one of four kinds. (1) The company's own figure, guidance or decision: "data center revenue was $39.1 billion, up 73%"; "management guided next quarter to $54 billion"; "the board approved a $50 billion buyback". (2) A customer's, supplier's, competitor's or partner's action with a size, date or name: "a cloud provider signed A100 contracts running into 2029"; "a national laboratory ordered two supercomputers built on Vera Rubin CPUs"; "TSMC said CoWoS capacity will double in 2026"; "a survey found executives will put 46% of accelerator budgets into domestic chips". (3) A named party's claim or estimate: "the CFO said A100s sold six years ago still run at full utilization"; "an analyst raised FY2027 EPS to $8.97"; "an investor accused hyperscalers of understating depreciation by $176 billion". (4) A policy or regulatory decision or step: "the Commerce Department approved H200 sales to China"; "Singapore charged four firms over server exports".
- Go through the item from its first paragraph to its last and take every statement of these kinds; a page with eight such statements yields eight evidence items, not a selection. Stop only at the end of the item.
- Reject everything else: a product, game, driver or benchmark detail without a size ("the expansion supports DLSS"; "the card draws 415W"); an investor's position or a share-price move ("he is short the stock"; "shares fell 13% this month"); an author's general risks or valuation arithmetic ("if AI pulls back it would hurt"; "at 34 times earnings the stock is worth $305"); the reporter's framing or background ("Gulf states have spent billions but still depend on the company"; "the A100 launched in 2020"); an expert's view on politics or strategy without a figure ("diversifying suppliers does not reduce political dependence"); the same fact or arrangement said again in other words: a release that describes one deployment in five sentences yields one evidence item, its figures ("up to 10x faster"; "40 data centers in 15 countries") a second and third; a quote that only characterizes ("a pivotal moment"; "heterogeneous inference"); company boilerplate, bylines, forward-looking-statement text.
- A statement's links name this answer's candidates it is evidence for (c1 …), or nothing; the open questions it bears on are filed by a separate step that reads them.

How to write evidence
- One evidence item records one statement. Copy its quote verbatim. Separately write a standalone summary in one_line: who did or said what, how much and for which period.
- Identify the speaker and, for a retelling, the original speaker and statement day. Use the schema's tier: fact for official actions, published actual figures or completed transactions; party_statement for company guidance, management statements or officials' remarks; third_party_view for analyst, media or expert opinions; rumour for unnamed-source or unattributed claims.
- Use only this item's information. Report plans as plans; do not infer committed funding, orders, deliveries or revenue.

Which questions to propose
- Open a candidate only for one of four reasons, named in opens_as. main_driver: an annual quantity that carries the company's value (the segment that carries the business, gross margin, capital spending), whether or not the company guides it; the question's ranges settle it, not a guidance figure. Not every reported or guided line. industry_aggregate: one aggregate quantity for one calendar year, such as the combined capital spending of named companies; a later estimate, another population or another wording of the same aggregate is evidence to the shown aggregate thesis. policy_stage: a stage of a policy process, with the authority that decides it named. binding_obligation: an obligation a universe company takes on in its own name (a guarantee, financing, an equity stake, a purchase commitment, a backstop of customers' capacity or revenue). Not yet signed: a yes/no question due on a day after the item by which the signing can be checked, at most 18 months out. Already taken on, as one deal or as a programme: a financing_amount question on the amount the obligation reaches at the company's next annual filing, settled by that filing's commitments note; the announcement itself is evidence to it.
- A number, a financial line, a target or a named customer project does not by itself open a thesis; a customer's deployment plan is evidence to the supplier's demand and product theses unless it changes the supplier's own cash or credit risk.
- For every candidate: settled_by names the public material that resolves it (an annual report, a filing's note, an official decision). A different population, source, estimate, wording or direction of a question is the same question; a different quantity, period or decision is another.
- A yearly metric asks for a quantity over a defined fiscal or calendar period and keeps the current/next-year limit. A milestone asks whether a specified event or project reaches a defined state by a deadline; a numeric completion target can define that state without becoming a yearly metric. Do not repackage a beyond-horizon annual forecast as an event. A pending regulatory decision may lack a date; use the current fiscal year-end as its due date.
- Do not propose theses about quarterly figures or guidance, undated subjects such as moats or strategy, executive appointments, shareholder votes or bylaws, routine litigation procedure, or buyback authorisations.

How to write a candidate thesis
- One thesis concerns one figure for a named period or one event. Separate independently meaningful outcomes.
- Write a question, not an assertion. A figure or event must be able to determine the outcome on the due date.
- A question about a company's revenue, profit, share or product progress is an asset thesis; put its ticker in object, even when policy or macroeconomics drives it. A theme thesis asks what happens in the world, such as licensing, interest rates or aggregate spending, rather than the resulting effect on one company.
- Write generated descriptions in English. Copy quote exactly from the source, without translation.
- Define concrete, verifiable conditions now. Do not propose a ladder whose thresholds depend on an unspecified future target.
- Use five rungs; only a yes/no question about an event has two. A numeric figure always gets five ranges, never a single threshold. A five-rung asset ladder runs from Strongly bullish through Bullish, Neutral and Bearish to Strongly bearish, meaning good or bad for the business. A theme ladder runs between two ends of an outcome range; label the outcomes, without assigning business sentiment. Conditions must not overlap or leave gaps: exactly one must hold when resolved. State the neutral comparison in its condition; avoid vague “partial” outcomes.
- Set the due date when the question can be resolved. For a figure, use its publication date. Company figures use the company's fiscal year: “this year” contains the item's publication day, and “next year” follows it. Other figures use calendar years. For an event, name the date at which its outcome is assessed.

Research groups
- A research group is one ongoing matter in the world that several questions track together: a product rollout and its customer deployments, a financing or acquisition deal, a policy process, an investment or demand cycle. It usually spans companies and themes. When a candidate tracks a matter, declare the group in new_groups (local id n1, n2 …, with a name, a scope that says what is happening, and aliases: the names the matter goes by in the press, such as product, project or programme names and the parties; not company names) and cite that id in group_refs; a declared group whose names match a stored group is that group. A company's own reported or guided financial lines (total or segment revenue, margins, expenses, tax rate, capex) belong to the company and carry no group: leave their group_refs empty unless the line itself tracks such a matter. A company is not a group, and a thesis is not a group.

Identity fields and numeric bounds
- Select the closest measure allowed by the schema. Scope is its actual segment, product, population or event subject. Reuse a supplied reference name only when it has the same meaning; leave scope empty when unqualified.
- period_start and period_end describe the period the figure covers. Convert fiscal years using the supplied fiscal-year note. Calendar year 2026 is 2026-01-01 through 2026-12-31. For an event, use the start of the year in which it is proposed through the due date.
- Identify the accounting basis and unit. For event or policy_event, select the event type; otherwise use n/a. The schema supplies the allowed values.
- Each numeric rung has an inclusive lower bound lo and exclusive upper bound hi, in the stated unit. Dollars are full dollar amounts; percentages use 73, not 0.73. The lowest numeric range has lo null, the highest hi null. Both bounds are null for yes/no outcomes.

[Subjects] The objects this item concerns: NVDA. For a candidate thesis about a company, object is its ticker; about a theme, choose an id from this list, or state what the matter is when none fits:
  - chip-export-controls: Chip export controls
  - ai-capex: AI capital spending
  - custom-silicon: Custom silicon at cloud providers
  - semiconductor-cycle: Semiconductor cycle
  - fed-policy-rate: Fed policy rate
  - us-inflation: US inflation
  - us-recession-risk: US recession risk
  - us-china-tariffs: US–China tariffs
  - taiwan-strait: Taiwan Strait
  - middle-east-conflict: Middle East conflict and oil prices
  - russia-ukraine-war: Russia–Ukraine war
  - supply-chain-shift: Supply-chain shift and shipping
Fiscal-year note (a numeric thesis takes its year and due date from it):
NVDA's fiscal year ends in month 1 and is named for the calendar year in which it ends: FY2027 runs from 2026-02 to 2027-01; the publication day 2026-07-05 falls in FY2027, so this year is FY2027 and next year is FY2028; FY2027's full-year figures are published in the annual report around 2027-02; use that day as the due date.

[What to read out] The author's forecasts, ratings and price targets with their figures; the facts and figures the author cites, with their original attribution. Not the author's general arguments or risk lists.

[Research reference] Existing quantities and scopes (measure[scope](event_type)). Reuse a name only when the meaning is the same; propose important questions outside the list as usual, with their actual scope:
  - NVDA: total_revenue; segment_revenue; gross_margin; operating_margin; operating_expense_growth; tax_rate; capex; product_revenue[Blackwell+Rubin]; product_revenue[Vera]; shipments_or_capacity[Rubin]; event[Rubin](shipment); event[Rubin](launch); event[H20/H200 China](licence); event[SK Telecom AI factory](deployment)

[Research groups] None yet. For a candidate that tracks an ongoing matter (a product rollout, a deal, a policy process, an investment or demand cycle), declare the group in new_groups (local ids n1, n2 …) and cite it in group_refs; leave group_refs empty for a company's own financial lines.

It's never fun to see your investments lose money. And when a stock's price falls more than 10% in a month, it's normal to wonder if you should sell to lock in your gains before it falls any further.
That's something investors in Nvidia ( NVDA +2.48% ) need to seriously think about. Shares of the world's leading chipmaker dropped 12.6% between June 2 and July 2, and they're down 17% from May's all-time high of $235.74/share.
But this latest drop might not be such a bad thing, actually. Here's why investors shouldn't panic and why Nvidia's pullback might actually be good news.
Image source: Nvidia.
There have always been ebbs and flows with Nvidia stock
Obviously, a pullback in a company's stock price offers new investors the opportunity to buy the dip. That's not the kind of "good news" I'm talking about here, although it's true that now might be a good moment to open a new position in the chipmaker if you don't already own shares.
Instead, I'm talking about the natural ebbs and flows of Nvidia's stock price. The company's road to being the largest company in the world with a $4.7 trillion market cap hasn't been a smooth one. In just the last five years, the stock has seen dizzying plunges multiple times.

Between November 2021 and October 2022, Nvidia's share price plunged 66%. It recovered a bit, only to drop by more than 20% again in December 2022. The company went on to experience nine drops of 15% or more between July 2023 and March 2026, about three per year.
But over the last five years, the stock has risen by more than 851%. And if you had sold during any one of those previous 15% dips, you would have missed out on lots of gains .
The biggest of those gains came suddenly and after a prolonged downturn. For example, between October 2025 and March 2026, Nvidia's stock lost 20% of its value over five months. Then, without warning, shares surged 42.7% between March 30 and May 14, hitting all-time highs.
Image source: Getty Images.
A roller-coaster ride
When a stock rockets upward and never experiences temporary pullbacks like Nvidia's has over the last five years, it can make new investors reluctant to buy shares out of concern that the stock is too expensive. And as the world's largest company by market cap, Nvidia already faces skepticism about its valuation.
It can also set the company up to experience a major share price drop if it reports anything less than stellar earnings. Nvidia doesn't seem to have that problem. In fact, it almost faces the opposite issue: Over the past two years, Nvidia's earnings reports have been stellar, with massive growth in revenue and net income. Yet after five of its last eight earnings reports, the stock has seen an immediate and significant share price decline .
If recent history is any guide, Nvidia's recent share price drop is likely to reverse itself unexpectedly, and the stock should soar to new heights . Smart investors know better than to panic sell this longtime winner that's still at the top of its game.
